lessons.title: Meet the board
lessons.summary: Read the coordinates and find your way around the 64 squares.

steps.text: The board has eight files, a through h, and eight ranks, 1 through 8. Each square has one coordinate, like e4.
Follow the moves by their starting and ending squares. White always moves first.
After e2 to e4, the pawn sits on e4. The small coordinate labels help you name every square.

steps.question: Which square is on file e and rank 4?
steps.explain: Files use letters and ranks use numbers, so the square is e4.

lessons.title: How the pieces move
lessons.summary: Learn the paths of pawns, knights, bishops, rooks, queens, and kings.

steps.text: Rooks travel in straight lines, bishops diagonally, and queens combine both paths. They cannot jump over other pieces.
Knights jump in an L shape. Bishops stay on the color of square where they began.

steps.hint: Move a pawn two squares forward from its starting square.
steps.wrongFeedback: Try a legal pawn move from e2 to e4.
steps.successFeedback: That is right. A pawn may move two squares on its first move.

steps.question: Which piece can jump over other pieces?
steps.explain: The knight is the only piece that jumps over pieces.

lessons.title: Check, checkmate, and stalemate
lessons.summary: Know when a king is threatened and when a game ends.

steps.text: Check means the king is attacked. The player must move the king, block the attack, or capture the attacker.
This quick game ends in checkmate: the king is in check and has no legal escape.
Stalemate is different: the player to move is not in check but has no legal move. The game is a draw.

steps.question: A player has no legal moves, but their king is not in check. What is it?
steps.explain: Without check, no legal moves means stalemate and a draw.

lessons.title: Castle to safety
lessons.summary: Use the king's special move to tuck it behind a rook.

steps.text: Castling moves the king two squares toward a rook, then places that rook on the square the king crossed.
White castles kingside; Black castles queenside. The king and rook must not have moved before.

steps.question: Can a king castle out of check?
options: Yes, if the rook has not moved
steps.explain: You cannot castle out of, through, or into check.

steps.text: The squares between king and rook must be empty, and neither piece may have moved earlier.

lessons.title: En passant
lessons.summary: Catch a pawn that just passed your pawn on its first move.

steps.text: If an enemy pawn moves two squares and lands beside yours, you may capture it as if it had moved one square.

steps.hint: The white pawn on e5 can capture the pawn that just passed it.
steps.wrongFeedback: Try the special diagonal capture from e5 to d6.
steps.successFeedback: Correct. En passant is recorded as a pawn capture on d6.

steps.text: This capture is only available immediately on the next move. If you wait, the chance is gone.

steps.question: When can you capture en passant?
options: Only on the move immediately after the two-square pawn move
steps.explain: En passant must be used immediately or it expires.

lessons.title: Promote a pawn
lessons.summary: Turn a pawn reaching the last rank into a powerful piece.

steps.text: When a pawn reaches the far side of the board, it must promote to a queen, rook, bishop, or knight.

steps.hint: Advance the pawn on a7 to the last rank. A queen is usually strongest.
steps.wrongFeedback: Move the pawn from a7 to a8 and choose a promoted piece.
steps.successFeedback: Nice. Promotion can create a queen, or another piece when that is more useful.

steps.text: The promotion piece is chosen as part of the pawn's move. Promotion to a queen is common.

steps.question: Must you promote to a queen?
options: No, you may choose a rook, bishop, or knight
No, the pawn stays a pawn
steps.explain: You may choose any of the four pieces, even if that choice is not a queen.

lessons.title: A guide to piece values
lessons.summary: Use simple values to compare exchanges and spot hanging pieces.

steps.text: A common guide is pawn 1, knight 3, bishop 3, rook 5, and queen 9. The king is priceless.

steps.question: You can trade a rook for a bishop. Which piece is usually worth more?
steps.explain: A rook is commonly valued around five points, compared with three for a bishop.

steps.text: These numbers are guides, not rules. A piece's safety, activity, and the position matter too.

steps.question: What should you check before taking a piece?
options: Whether it is defended and what can capture back
Whether it is near the edge
steps.explain: Count defenders and attackers so a tempting capture does not lose material.

lessons.title: Control the center
lessons.summary: Central squares give your pieces more room and influence.

steps.text: The central squares e4, d4, e5, and d5 are valuable. Pieces placed near the center can often reach more of the board.
A central pawn claims space. Knights and other pieces can support or challenge that space.

steps.hint: Move one of the two central pawns two squares.
steps.wrongFeedback: Try e2 to e4 or d2 to d4 to claim the center.
steps.successFeedback: Good. Either central pawn move is a sound way to begin fighting for space.

steps.question: Why are central squares useful?
options: They give pieces influence over more squares
steps.explain: A central piece usually controls more routes and can switch sides more quickly.

lessons.title: Develop and castle
lessons.summary: Bring pieces into the game, then secure your king.

steps.text: Development means moving your knights and bishops from their starting squares to useful, active squares.
Develop pieces toward the center and castle to bring your king to safety.

steps.question: Which plan is a strong opening habit?
options: Bring the queen out first every time
steps.explain: Develop knights and bishops, contest the center, and castle when it is safe.

steps.text: Avoid launching an attack before your pieces can help. A developed team can defend and attack together.

lessons.title: A back-rank checkmate
lessons.summary: Spot a king trapped behind its own pawns.

steps.text: A king on its back rank can be trapped by its own pawns. A rook or queen may be able to deliver mate along that rank.

steps.hint: The rook can travel up the e-file and attack the king across the back rank.
steps.wrongFeedback: Look for a rook move to e8. The king has no safe square behind its pawns.
steps.successFeedback: Checkmate. The rook checks along the eighth rank while the pawns block the king's escape.

steps.text: Back-rank danger is a reason to create luft: a safe pawn move can give your king an escape square.

steps.question: What often traps a king in a back-rank mate?
steps.explain: Its own pawns can block every escape square behind it.

lessons.title: Find a fork
lessons.summary: Attack two targets at once with one move.

steps.text: A fork is one move that attacks two or more enemy pieces at the same time. Knights are especially good at forking.
Look for a move that creates two threats. Your opponent may save one target, but not both.

steps.question: What makes a move a fork?
options: It attacks two or more targets at once
It protects the king by castling
steps.explain: The double attack forces the opponent to choose which threat to answer.

steps.text: Before moving, check whether your piece will attack the king and another valuable target together.

lessons.title: Pins and the king + rook mate idea
lessons.summary: Restrict a piece with a pin, then learn the basic rook-and-king plan.

steps.text: A pin happens when a piece cannot safely move because doing so would expose a more valuable piece or the king behind it.
Here the rook and king share a file. A rook can pin an enemy piece to its king along a rank, file, or diagonal.
In king-and-rook versus king, use your king to help. Drive the opposing king toward an edge, then use the rook to cut off escape squares.
The rook takes away a rank, while your king controls nearby squares. Keep the rook protected as you shrink the box.

steps.question: What helps you checkmate with king and rook?
options: Use your king to support the rook and restrict the enemy king
Chase the enemy king with the rook alone
steps.explain: The king supports the rook, which cuts off escape squares and drives the enemy king to an edge.
